newsitem.title: GERMANY: TENNIS-GRAF CONSIDERS ENDING INJURY-PLAGUED CAREER.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-GRAF CONSIDERS ENDING INJURY-PLAGUED CAREER.

text.p: Steffi Graf, worried that chronic injuries could damage her long-term health, said at the weekend she is considering retiring from the game and would have no problem ending her career.

The German winner of 21 grand slam tennis titles in an unparalleled 15-year career also told Welt am Sonntag newspaper that she was unhappy over the treatment she has received from one of her doctors.

Graf, who celebrated her 28th birthday in a physiotherapy clinic on Saturday, said the physician, Dr Hans Paessler, had failed to warn her about the dangers of returning to tournament play before a knee injury had fully healed.
"I am completely open on this question," said Graf about retirement when the newspaper's interviewer asked about the possibility.
"I am hopeful of the abilities of the physicians to enable me to continue playing, but I would have no problem ending my career."

One of the most successful tennis players ever, Graf was long the world's number one ranked player. After 94 consecutive weeks on top she slipped to second behind Martina Hingis in April and recently fell to third due in part to a three-month lay-off because of an injury to the same left knee.
She returned to competition in May, but fared poorly in a tournament in Berlin and at the French Open in early June when she failed to reach the last four for the first time in more than a decade.
Less than two weeks later, in an operation shrouded in secrecy, Graf had surgery on her left knee in Vienna and is expected to be sidelined for up to six months.

"I would have no problem ending my career if the doctors can't (restore my health)," said Graf, who has won Wimbledon seven times and won all four grand slam tournaments -- as well as the Olympic gold medal -- in 1988.

"I have tried everything possible. But even if I can't play tennis any more, I always want to be able to move about, to remain active in sport. That is important for me. I am open to the question about the end of my career. I'm not at all afraid."
Graf, recovering at a physiotherapy clinic in Gars outside Vienna, said she would not rush a comeback. She has been sidelined by a total of 43 injuries in her professional career that began in 1982.

"I want to know what risks I will be running if I return to tennis and how I can become completely healthy again," Graf said. "I want to remain healthy enough after my career to be able to do other things. That is why I had this operation." Graf said she was annoyed her Heidelberg physician, Paessler, had failed to warn her about the dangers of returning. She also suggested she had not yet ruled out legal action.

"He assured me and my coach Heinz Guenthardt on several occasions between the tournaments in Strasbourg and Berlin that nothing could happen (to her knee) and that the situation could not worsen. I play in the tournaments and the cartilage breaks. Whose fault is that?"
She was also critical of Paessler for discussing her medical files in public.
"I did not release him from his oath of confidentiality and he has nevertheless been discussing my health files in public. I consider that not proper."

Long the darling of German sport, Graf has endured several years of intense media scrutiny over her tax affairs. Her father Peter Graf was convicted of evading 12 million marks on her earnings earlier this year and sentenced to nine months in jail.
Graf was herself also under investigation until German prosecutors dropped a parallel tax evasion query.
